options: Pick the most capable model and build a demo on a handful of emails, then gather requirements from the reactions to the demo in follow-up meetings
Draft the full architecture from experience with similar clients and present it for sign-off together with a delivery date
Run structured discovery: map the workflow and volumes, find owners, data and error costs, record baselines, and agree success measures before any model is chosen
Start with the cheapest model and tune its prompt on the COO's examples until the COO says the answers look good
questions.explanation: Discovery comes before design. The architect needs the problem statement, the current workflow and volumes, who decides and who can veto, what data is involved and how sensitive it is, what each kind of error costs, the constraints, and baseline numbers and success measures. A demo-first or model-first approach anchors the project on whatever the demo happens to show, a pre-written architecture hardens assumptions nobody has checked, and tuning on one executive's examples optimizes for a sample of one opinion. (Delivery practice.)
questions.whyTested: Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering.

questions.question: Stakeholders agreed that the assistant should 'answer accurately and quickly'. Six weeks into the build, security demands EU-only processing and legal requires an audit trail, and both change the design. Which discovery practice would have avoided this?
options: Eliciting non-functional requirements explicitly (latency, accuracy, residency, retention, auditability) and naming security and legal in a RACI
Choosing a model with a larger context window, so that later requirements can be absorbed without a redesign of the architecture, the data flows or the hosting platform
Adding more reviewers to the team after launch, so that the extra compliance work is absorbed by people instead of by changes to the design and the project plan
Asking the model itself to list every regulation that might apply, and building to that list from the start of the project
questions.explanation: Stakeholders rarely volunteer 'p95 under 3 seconds' or 'EU-only processing'. Discovery has to draw out the non-functional requirements and identify everyone with a veto (security, legal, compliance, operations) early, for example in a RACI matrix, because residency and audit needs change model choice, platform and architecture. A larger window, more reviewers or a model-generated checklist do not replace asking the people who own the constraints. (Delivery practice.)
questions.whyTested: Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering: non-functional requirements and veto holders.

questions.question: A sponsor says the pilot will be approved 'if it feels good'. The architect wants a formulation that settles disputes with evidence. Which acceptance criterion is best?
options: Reviewers should find the answers generally good by the time the pilot ends, as judged by the sponsor and the project team
The assistant should look clearly better than the previous prototype in most of the live demonstrations given to leadership and to the pilot team
Average satisfaction from the pilot team should be above four stars out of five in the end-of-pilot survey
95 percent of 500 representative cases correct, no critical-severity errors, p95 latency under 4 seconds, agreed before the build
questions.explanation: Good criteria are specific, measurable, achievable and relevant, expressed as thresholds on a held-out evaluation set that mirrors real traffic, and agreed with the sponsor before the build so that the evaluation suite becomes the acceptance test. 'Generally good', 'looks better' and a friendly team's rating are opinions that cannot settle a dispute. Even softer topics such as safety can be quantified, for example as the share of outputs flagged in a large trial.
questions.whyTested: Manage expectation alignment: measurable acceptance criteria.

questions.question: A sponsor wants a go decision. The proposal compares the monthly model bill with the staff hours saved if the assistant handles every ticket, yet in practice people will review 30 percent of the outputs. Which business case is most defensible?
options: Show the monthly token bill against hours saved assuming full automation, using one optimistic figure so that the decision is easy to make
Show cost per completed task, including review time and running costs, against measured baselines, as a range with sensitivity analysis
Compare the model's price per million tokens with a competitor's price list and recommend whichever vendor is cheaper for the expected monthly volume
Postpone cost modeling until after launch, when the real invoices will make the numbers certain for everyone
questions.explanation: A defensible case compares total cost of ownership per completed task, which includes model usage, retrieval and infrastructure, integration and evaluation work, human review time, monitoring, support and change management, with baseline numbers measured before the build. Present ranges and state the assumptions, because a single optimistic figure collapses when review rates or volumes differ. Token price alone is often a minority of the total in high-oversight workflows, and postponing the model leaves the sponsor deciding blind. (Delivery practice.)
questions.whyTested: Communicate trade-offs: business-case framing with total cost and measured baselines.

questions.question: A department head is alarmed that the assistant worded the same answer differently on two days, and demands that it behave 'like a calculator'. What is the best response?
options: Promise that setting the sampling temperature to zero makes every output identical from one run to the next, so the behavior can be signed off by the department head this week
Explain that the variation is a defect that the vendor is expected to remove in an upcoming model release, and ask for patience until then
Explain that wording can vary between runs, agree which parts must stay stable, enforce them with schemas and validators, and measure consistency on an evaluation set
Replace generation with a fixed library of canned answers and stop using the model for this task altogether, accepting the loss of flexibility
questions.explanation: Language models can word the same answer differently, which is a property to design around, not a bug to apologize for. Agree with the stakeholder what must be stable (facts, decisions, format), enforce structure with schemas and validators, and treat consistency as an acceptance criterion measured on an evaluation set. A promise of identical output cannot rest on a setting: recent models reject non-default temperature, top_p and top_k values with a 400 error, and structured outputs guarantee schema conformance, not identical wording. Canned answers throw away the value of the solution.
questions.whyTested: Communicate non-determinism and limits to stakeholders.

questions.question: Before a pilot of a clinical-documentation assistant, a skeptical physician asks, 'Can it be wrong?' Which way of setting expectations is best?
options: Show measured error rates and types on representative cases, with real failures, and say which errors validation catches and which need review
Reassure the physician with the vendor's published benchmark scores for the model, including its results on medical knowledge and clinical reasoning tests
Say that errors are very rare because the testing was thorough, and offer to discuss the details with the physician after the pilot has ended
Show only the best demonstrations so that the physician sees what the assistant can do at its peak, then let the pilot reveal how it performs in everyday use
questions.explanation: Expectation setting works when it is concrete and honest: show how often and in what ways the system is wrong on cases like the physician's own, which failures are caught automatically, and what the human must still check. General benchmarks do not describe this workload, reassurance without numbers invites distrust or over-reliance, and a best-case demo sets an expectation the system will break. For clinical content, review by a qualified person stays part of the design.
questions.whyTested: Manage expectation alignment: communicate limits with evidence.

questions.question: Eighteen months after launch, a new engineer asks why the team chose a mid-tier model, prompt caching and US-only inference, and proposes switching to a newer model. Which artifact best preserves the reasoning?
options: The team chat history from the design period, which is searchable by keyword and shows who argued for each choice and when
The commit messages in the repository, which show when each setting changed and which engineer changed it
The system's model card, which describes its intended use, evaluation results by slice and known limits
A set of architecture decision records: context, options, criteria, the choice, consequences and when to revisit, kept beside the design
questions.explanation: An architecture decision record captures one significant decision with its context, the options weighed, the criteria, the choice and its consequences, and a trigger for revisiting it, so the reasoning survives staff changes and can be re-run when a newer model ships. Chat history and commit messages hold fragments without the trade-offs, and a model card documents what the system is and where it fails, not why each design choice was made. (Delivery practice.)
questions.whyTested: Document architectures and communicate architectural decisions.

questions.question: Two architects disagree about using a workflow or an agent loop for a claims process, and each argues from personal experience. Which technique best moves the decision forward?
options: Let the more senior architect decide, because experience is the fastest way to resolve a disagreement between two capable people
Agree weighted criteria with stakeholders first, score both options, then check whether the winner changes when the weights move, and record the decision in writing
Build both options in full and compare them with real traffic after launch before deciding which one to keep running
Take a vote among the engineers on the team and record the result as the decision, with a note of the dissenting views
questions.explanation: A decision matrix turns preferences into explicit trade-offs: criteria such as accuracy, latency, cost, auditability and effort are weighted with stakeholders before any scoring, so nobody tunes the weights to favor a favorite, and a sensitivity check shows whether the conclusion is robust. Seniority and votes substitute authority or popularity for evidence, and building both in full spends the project's budget on the decision. (Delivery practice.)
questions.whyTested: Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs.

questions.question: Sales wants to promise customers 99.95 percent monthly availability for an assistant whose answer path depends on the Claude API on the standard tier, a vendor CRM and a search index. Which approach is most sound?
options: Buy a Priority Tier commitment, which guarantees that the Claude API will be available whenever the assistant needs it, then promise 99.95 percent on that basis
Promise 99.95 percent and rely on service credits from the vendors if one of the dependencies fails
Base the commitment on the weakest dependency and your fallbacks, set an internal SLO tighter than the SLA, and promise no more than that supports
Offer no availability commitment at all, since model behavior cannot be guaranteed for any customer, and let each customer deal be negotiated separately
questions.explanation: An SLA should promise only what the architecture and its least reliable dependency can sustain, backed by retries, queueing, cached or reduced answers and human handoff, with a tighter internal SLO as an early warning. The standard tier is best-effort, and new Priority Tier capacity commitments are no longer sold; where one exists it targets uptime for committed capacity rather than guaranteeing it. Vendor credits do not repair a customer relationship, and refusing any commitment is rarely acceptable to customers.
questions.whyTested: Manage expectation alignment, including SLAs.

questions.question: A retailer will launch its assistant to two million customers on Monday after testing with 500 users. The expected peak is about forty times the test load, and the previous day's traffic will be near zero. Which plan best avoids a launch-day wave of 429 errors?
options: Estimate peak requests and tokens against rate limits, ask for higher limits early, use caching, and ramp traffic in stages behind a feature flag
Rely on SDK retries with exponential backoff, and expect the extra attempts to absorb the surge as it builds during the first morning
Move the chat traffic to the Batch API, which has its own limits and a lower price per token, so launch-day load is spread over the day
Launch to everyone at once, so that the request for higher limits is justified by real demand and the provider sees the actual peak
questions.explanation: Capacity planning compares expected peak requests and tokens with rate limits, spend caps and budgets before launch. Limits are maximums rather than guaranteed minimums, and a sharp jump from near-zero traffic can trigger acceleration limits that return 429 errors, so ramp gradually and ask for increases early. For most models, cached input reads do not count toward the input-token limit. Retries smooth short bursts but not a sustained overshoot, and batch processing is for latency-tolerant work, not live chat.
questions.whyTested: Support lifecycle phases: capacity planning before launch.

questions.question: At 3 pm every request starts failing with HTTP 429. Request volume looks normal, the response carries no retry-after header, and the error body contains the code enforced_spend_limit_reached. What should the incident runbook conclude?
options: A per-minute rate limit was exceeded, so the service should back off for a few seconds and retry the request, honoring the suggested delay
The API is overloaded across all users, so the service should wait for capacity to return and then resume sending traffic
An API key has expired, so the key should be rotated and the service redeployed with the new key after the security team has approved the change
The organization hit its tier's monthly spend cap, so retries fail until access resumes or the limit is raised; request an increase
questions.explanation: A 429 with no retry-after header and the code enforced_spend_limit_reached means the organization has reached its tier's monthly spend cap. Usage stays paused until the first day of the next month (00:00 UTC) unless a higher limit is arranged, so backing off and the SDK's automatic retries cannot help. An ordinary rate limit carries a retry-after header, overload is a 529, and an expired key returns a 401. The runbook should cover raising the limit and alerting on spend well before the cap.
questions.whyTested: Incident handling: recognize the failure mode before choosing the response.

questions.question: A pilot ran with the company's most enthusiastic power users and reported 94 percent satisfaction. The sponsor wants to roll out to 3,000 staff next month. What is the main weakness of the evidence?
options: The pilot used too many users, so the satisfaction figure is too precise to be trusted and should be discarded in favor of a smaller sample
The group is unrepresentative and nothing was measured against a baseline or agreed thresholds, so results at scale will likely be worse
Pilots should run without human oversight, so that reviewers cannot influence the measured quality of the assistant's answers
Satisfaction is irrelevant to a rollout decision, because only the token cost per request matters when thousands of staff use it
questions.explanation: Enthusiasts forgive flaws and use the tool well, so their satisfaction overstates what 3,000 ordinary staff will see. A pilot is evidence only if participants represent the real population and outcomes are compared with baseline numbers and acceptance criteria set beforehand. Extra oversight in a pilot is normal, satisfaction is one useful signal among accuracy, time saved and error severity, and cost is not the only measure. (Delivery practice.)
questions.whyTested: Support lifecycle phases: pilot design and feedback loops.

questions.question: The plan moves the assistant from pilot to production on Friday. The evaluation suite still shows an unresolved class of critical-severity errors, but the sponsor is eager to ship. How does a phase gate help here?
options: It lets the project ship on schedule and fix the critical errors during hypercare, because gates should never be allowed to delay a committed date
It lets the team lower the evaluation threshold until the suite passes, so that the planned date holds and the sponsor stays satisfied
Criteria agreed in advance make go or no-go a measurement: hold the release, or let the accountable owner record a formal risk acceptance
It lets the architect override the sponsor and cancel the project whenever any known error remains in the evaluation results
questions.explanation: A phase gate checks agreed criteria (evaluation results, security review, operational readiness, budget) before work moves on, so the decision rests on evidence instead of enthusiasm. If a critical failure class is still open, the options are to hold, or for the accountable owner to accept the risk explicitly and on the record. Hypercare is for the tail of small issues, not for known critical errors; lowering the bar after seeing results defeats the gate; and a gate informs the decision rather than handing the architect a veto over the sponsor. (Delivery practice.)
questions.whyTested: Support lifecycle phases: phase gates between pilot and production.

questions.question: The day before go-live, dashboards exist, but nobody is on call, rollback has never been tried and the incident runbook is a draft. What should the architect recommend?
options: Treat the readiness review as not passed: assign on-call, test rollback and drill the runbook first, with early access limited to a small flagged cohort
Launch to everyone as planned, because the existing dashboards show that the system is being monitored well enough for a first release
Launch on schedule, and have the build team work out the rollback steps and the runbook if an incident actually occurs
Cancel the launch and restart discovery from the beginning, since operational gaps prove the original design was wrong
questions.explanation: An operational readiness review is the last gate before go-live: monitoring and alerts, runbooks, on-call ownership, rollback, capacity, security sign-off, training and support must all exist. Dashboards without an owner, an untested rollback and a draft runbook mean nobody can respond when something breaks. The right move is to close the gaps (a limited, flagged cohort with hypercare can proceed once on-call and rollback work) rather than ship blind or discard the design. (Delivery practice.)
questions.whyTested: Support lifecycle phases: handoff and operational readiness.

questions.question: An email from Anthropic says the model your production service pins will be retired in about two months, and names a recommended replacement. Which plan is best?
options: Wait until the last week, then change the model string, since the replacement is newer and will certainly be better than the model it replaces
Inventory usage, read the migration notes, adapt code and prompts, compare old and new on the evaluation suite, canary behind a flag, cut over early
Switch every environment to the largest available model today without testing, to be safe from any further retirements in the future
Ask support to postpone the retirement for your account, and plan nothing until they answer, so that no engineering time is spent meanwhile
questions.explanation: A deprecated model keeps working until its retirement date, after which requests fail; Anthropic gives at least 60 days' notice for publicly released models and names a replacement. The plan is a migration, not a string change: find every use (the Console usage export breaks usage down by API key and model), read what changed for the replacement (rejected parameters, defaults, token counts), run your evaluations side by side, shadow or canary, and keep rollback ready. Waiting leaves no time to fix regressions, an untested jump to a bigger model risks cost and behavior surprises, and a postponement is not something to plan around.
questions.whyTested: Support lifecycle phases: versioning and model deprecation.

questions.question: A team moved a service from Claude Sonnet 4.5 to Claude Sonnet 5.5 by changing only the model ID. Some calls now fail with 400 errors, and the monthly cost is noticeably higher for the same traffic. What did the migration miss?
options: Raising the organization's rate limits, since a shortage of capacity caused both the errors and the higher cost of the service
Wrapping every call in a retry loop, which resolves 400 responses and trims the cost of repeated attempts after each failed call
Removing settings the new model rejects (prefill, thinking budgets, non-default sampling), recounting tokens, setting effort, rerunning evaluations
Pinning the old model again for good, since newer models cannot run prompts that were written for earlier ones without being rewritten
questions.explanation: Changing the model ID alone is rarely enough. Claude Sonnet 5.5 returns 400 errors for an assistant prefill and for a thinking token budget, and recent models reject non-default temperature, top_p and top_k values; thinking now runs by default on requests that did not set it; and the same text produces roughly 30 percent more tokens than on Claude Sonnet 4.5, which raises cost and affects output limits. Retries do not fix a malformed request, rate limits are unrelated, and going back is only a short bridge because the old model has a published retirement date.
questions.whyTested: Support lifecycle phases: model migration.

questions.question: A support assistant's quality dropped on Tuesday. Its prompt lives in a database row that three people edit in an admin console, and nothing records who changed what or when. Which practice would have made diagnosis and recovery fast?
options: Forbidding any prompt change after launch, so that the prompt can never be the cause of a quality drop, and requiring a director to approve exceptions
Tracking only daily token usage per request type, since a quality drop always shows up as a visible change in usage
Adding more reviewers to the support team, so that a quality drop is noticed sooner the next time it happens to a customer, and sharing the findings in a weekly report
Managing prompts, templates and settings as reviewed, versioned artifacts, with a release tag logged on every request and rollback available
questions.explanation: Prompts are production code. With versioned, reviewed and tested prompts, a release tag recorded on every request and a rollback path, a Tuesday drop can be tied to a specific change within minutes and reverted. Editing live text in place leaves no history, a freeze blocks needed fixes, token usage does not measure answer quality, and more reviewers improve detection but not diagnosis. (Delivery practice.)
questions.whyTested: Support lifecycle phases: prompt versioning and iteration.

questions.question: A harmful answer from the public chatbot is spreading on social media. Which response plan best fits a prepared incident runbook?
options: Triage severity, contain with a flag or kill switch, update stakeholders, trace the cause via request IDs and logged versions, fix, add a regression case
Delete the related logs to limit what can be shared any further, and wait for the attention to fade before saying anything
Publicly state that the model vendor is responsible for the answer, and change nothing until the vendor replies
Deny that the answer came from the product until the investigation has been completed in full and approved by legal counsel
questions.explanation: A prepared runbook turns panic into steps: assess severity, contain the behavior quickly (a feature flag or kill switch is why you keep them), tell stakeholders the facts and the actions, find the cause using the request IDs and the prompt and model versions logged on every request, fix, add the case to the regression set, and hold a blameless review. Deleting logs destroys the evidence you need, deflecting to the vendor ignores that the solution owner is accountable, and denial erodes trust when it is disproved. (Delivery practice.)
questions.whyTested: Support lifecycle phases: incident handling and communication.

questions.question: An excellent internal assistant launched six months ago, but only 12 percent of the target staff use it, although the technical dashboards are green. What is the most likely gap and the best fix?
options: The model is too weak, so the team should upgrade to the newest tier and relaunch the assistant with a company-wide announcement
Change management was missing: engage teams early, train them, name champions, open a feedback channel, phase adoption
Staff lack discipline, so usage should be mandated by policy and non-users reported to their managers each month
The assistant lacks features, so the team should add more tools and integrations before telling anyone about it again, this time with a bigger launch event
questions.explanation: Technical success with unprepared users still fails. Adoption follows people's trust and habits: engage the affected teams early, train them on what the assistant does well and badly, name champions who share concrete wins, give them a place to report problems, phase the rollout and measure adoption alongside quality. Claude Code's champion and communications kits illustrate the pattern. Green dashboards say nothing about whether people use the tool, and upgrading, mandating or adding features addresses guesses instead of the cause.
questions.whyTested: Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment: change management.

questions.question: Reviewers correct about 15 percent of the assistant's drafts, but the corrections vanish after sending. The sponsor asks how quality will improve over time. What is the best feedback loop?
options: Run a quarterly satisfaction survey of all staff and share the results with the team in a slide deck at the next planning meeting
Expect the assistant to learn from the reviewers' corrections automatically between conversations, because it sees every edit that is made
Capture each correction with its input, draft and reason code in an evaluation set, and review it on a schedule to drive changes
Ask reviewers to write free-form notes in a shared document, and read the notes at the annual review of the project
questions.explanation: A feedback loop needs captured, structured signals and a cadence that turns them into action. Reviewer corrections are the best labeled data you will get: stored with context and a reason they become the evaluation set and the backlog for prompt, retrieval or tool changes, and trend reports keep sponsors aligned. The model does not learn between conversations by itself, surveys are too coarse, and unstructured notes read once a year are lost.
questions.whyTested: Manage stakeholder feedback loops.

questions.question: Three months after launch, accuracy on sampled production traffic has slipped from 94 to 89 percent although no code changed. Which lifecycle practice detects and handles this best?
options: A yearly architecture review that revisits the original design assumptions with the whole team
Waiting for complaints to arrive, since users are the best detectors of any loss of quality in a deployed assistant
Redeploying the same release to reset it, then closing the ticket once the dashboards look normal again for a day
Monitor sampled quality against the acceptance thresholds, alert on a breach, investigate inputs and retrieval, and rerun the regression suite
questions.explanation: Quality can drift without any code change: the mix of questions shifts, source documents are refreshed, or a dependency behaves differently. The monitoring and iteration phase samples production traffic, scores it against the acceptance criteria, alerts on a breach, diagnoses the cause and feeds a planned iteration. Annual reviews and complaints are too slow and incomplete, and redeploying the same release changes nothing.
questions.whyTested: Support lifecycle phases: monitoring and iteration.

questions.question: The build team is handing a production assistant to operations. Which three items belong in the handoff package? (Choose three.)
options: Runbooks for likely situations (a burst of 429 errors, a harmful output, a model retirement), tested in a drill
The evaluation suite, dashboards and alert thresholds, with prompt and model release tags recorded on every request
A named owner list with escalation contacts, a data-flow diagram, and system documentation covering intended use, limits and known failure modes
The build engineers' personal API keys, shared in a team document, so that operations can call the model in an emergency
A single verbal walkthrough of the design, because written documents go stale and nobody reads them
questions.explanation: A handoff transfers the ability to operate, change and defend the system: tested runbooks, the evaluation suite and dashboards with release tags that tie behavior to versions, named owners and escalation paths, plus a data-flow diagram and a system document (a model card) that say what the system is for and where it fails. Sharing personal keys breaks identity and offboarding rules, and a one-time talk cannot be audited or repeated. (Delivery practice.)
questions.whyTested: Document architectures and provide implementation guidance.

questions.question: Which two practices make a pilot's results a trustworthy basis for a rollout decision? (Choose two.)
options: Choose participants who represent the real user population, not only enthusiastic volunteers
Measure outcomes against baseline numbers and acceptance criteria agreed before the pilot started
Define what counts as success after the results are in, so that the criteria fit what was achieved
Remove all human oversight during the pilot so that the raw performance of the model is visible
Limit the pilot to the team that built the assistant, because they understand its quirks best
questions.explanation: A pilot is evidence only when the sample looks like the eventual users and the yardstick was fixed beforehand and compared with a measured baseline. Setting criteria after the fact lets the result define the test, removing oversight in a live pilot adds risk without adding insight, and the builders are the least representative users. (Delivery practice.)
questions.whyTested: Support lifecycle phases: pilot design.

questions.question: Which two actions are part of change management for rolling out a Claude-based assistant to a large workforce? (Choose two.)
options: Name champions in each team and give people a single channel for questions and feedback
Train users on what the assistant does well and where it can be wrong, and phase adoption by group
Announce the launch by email and measure success only by whether the servers stay up
Keep the assistant's limits out of communications so that users are not discouraged
Switch off the previous process on launch day so that nobody has a fallback
questions.explanation: Change management is the people side of a rollout: champions and a visible feedback channel make adoption social and give problems a place to land, and honest training with phased adoption sets accurate expectations. Uptime says nothing about use, hiding limits sets users up for disappointment, and removing the fallback turns every flaw into an outage. (Delivery practice.)
questions.whyTested: Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment.

questions.question: Monitoring shows that a scheduled agent on Claude Managed Agents sent customer data to an unknown address after reading a poisoned ticket. Which three actions belong in the first response? (Choose three.)
options: Interrupt the running session and pause the deployment, so that no new scheduled run starts
Rotate any key or credential the agent could use, at the service that issued it
Copy the session's events to your own logs before anything is archived or deleted
Delete the session straight away so that the poisoned ticket cannot be read again
Archive the agent definition, which also stops any of its sessions that are already running
questions.explanation: Contain first: send an interrupt to the running session and pause the scheduled deployment so nothing new starts, then rotate any key the agent could reach, because an interrupt does not undo what it already did or sent. Preserve the session's events in your own logs before archiving or deleting, since deletion removes the record. Archiving an agent does not stop its running sessions, and a running session cannot be archived or deleted until it goes idle.
questions.whyTested: Incident handling for agent systems.

questions.question: The Claude API intermittently returns overloaded errors during peak hours, and the assistant is customer-facing. Which three measures belong in the degradation plan? (Choose three.)
options: Retry transient errors with exponential backoff, honoring any retry-after header
Serve cached or reduced answers, or queue work for later, and hand off to a person where needed
Tell users clearly when they are in a degraded mode, and test the fallback paths before launch
Retry immediately in a tight loop without limit until a call succeeds
Hide the degraded state from users so that confidence in the product is not shaken
questions.explanation: Graceful degradation plans a reduced but acceptable experience for each failing dependency: bounded retries with backoff for transient errors, cached or reduced answers, queuing and human handoff as fallbacks, honest status messages, and tests that prove the fallbacks work before they are needed. Unbounded tight retries amplify the overload, and hiding the degraded mode misleads users.
questions.whyTested: Manage expectation alignment, including SLAs: designing for dependency failure.

questions.question: For publicly released models, Anthropic notifies customers with active deployments at least 60 days before a model is retired.
questions.explanation: Anthropic's model deprecations page commits to at least 60 days' notice before retirement of publicly released models, by email and in the documentation. A deprecated model still works until its retirement date, after which requests fail, so the notice period is the planning window for migration.
questions.whyTested: Support lifecycle phases: model deprecation notice.

questions.question: Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud retire Claude models on the same dates as the first-party Claude API, so one retirement notice covers every deployment.
questions.explanation: The dates on Anthropic's deprecation page apply to Anthropic-operated platforms (the Claude API, Claude Platform on AWS and Microsoft Foundry). Partner-operated platforms such as Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud set their own retirement schedules, so the lifecycle owner must check each platform's model table separately.
questions.whyTested: Support lifecycle phases: versioning across platforms.

questions.question: New Priority Tier capacity commitments are no longer sold, so an availability plan should not depend on buying one and should rely on retries, fallbacks and headroom instead.
questions.explanation: Existing commitments run to the end of their contract, but new ones are not offered, and the standard tier is best-effort. Design for transient overload with backoff, graceful degradation and spare capacity, and size any SLA to what that design can sustain.
questions.whyTested: Manage expectation alignment, including SLAs.

questions.question: A proof of concept that worked on real data can go to production as it is, because it already proved the idea.
questions.explanation: A proof of concept answers a few risky questions about feasibility and value, usually without evaluation depth, security review, monitoring, runbooks or support. Moving to production needs the later lifecycle phases: pilot, phase gates and operational readiness. (Delivery practice.)
questions.whyTested: Support lifecycle phases: proof of concept versus production.

questions.question: An internal service level objective is usually set tighter than the external SLA, so the team is alerted before a customer commitment is at risk.
questions.explanation: The SLO is the working target (for example a share of answers within a time limit) and the SLA is the contractual promise with consequences. The gap is the early-warning margin, and an error budget derived from the SLO tells teams when to prioritize stability over new releases. (Delivery practice.)
questions.whyTested: Manage expectation alignment, including SLAs.

questions.question: The model usage bill is normally the complete cost of ownership of a Claude-based workflow.
questions.explanation: Total cost of ownership also includes retrieval and infrastructure, integration and engineering, evaluation, human review time, monitoring and support, and training and change management. In high-oversight workflows tokens are often a minority of the total, so a business case built on tokens alone misleads. (Delivery practice.)
questions.whyTested: Communicate trade-offs: business-case framing.

questions.question: Interrupting a running agent session undoes the actions it has already taken and recalls data it has already sent.
questions.explanation: An interrupt stops further model output (a running tool call may still finish), but it cannot reverse completed actions or recall data that has been sent. Incident response therefore also rotates credentials, pauses schedules, preserves evidence and assesses the impact.
questions.whyTested: Incident handling for agent systems.

questions.question: A feature flag lets a team switch a prompt version or model on for chosen users or percentages without redeploying, and doubles as a kill switch for risky behavior.
questions.explanation: Flags separate deployment from release: a new prompt or model can be exposed to a canary share, compared on quality and cost, and turned off in seconds if something goes wrong, which is why flags appear in both rollout plans and incident runbooks. (Delivery practice.)
questions.whyTested: Support lifecycle phases: controlled rollout and rollback.

questions.question: Because newer models can reject parameters that older code sets, moving to a new model needs a test against its migration notes, not just a changed model ID.
questions.explanation: Examples from the current migration guides: assistant prefill, thinking token budgets and non-default sampling values return 400 errors on recent models, defaults such as thinking can change, and token counts differ. Treat every model move as a small project with an evaluation run, not a configuration edit.
questions.whyTested: Support lifecycle phases: model migration.

lessons.title: From Business Problem to Architecture: Patterns and Value
lessons.summary: Turning a business sentence into an input, processing, output and feedback design; choosing between an augmented call, a workflow and an agent; and tying each decision to business value.
lessons.reading:
Every Claude solution starts as a business sentence, such as 'cut the time staff spend answering shipping-exception emails'. The architect's first job is to turn it into a design with four parts: what goes in (the input and the data it needs), what processing happens (model calls, tools, retrieval), what comes out (a draft, a decision, a record) and how the system learns (the feedback loop). Before choosing a pattern, run a quick fit assessment: is the input language-shaped, can a wrong answer be tolerated or caught, and can results be verified? The answers decide how much autonomy and how many checks the design needs.

Anthropic describes a ladder of patterns. The basic building block is the augmented LLM: one model call that can retrieve information, call tools and keep notes. Above it sit workflows, in which your code decides the path. Prompt chaining runs fixed steps in sequence with programmatic gates between them. Routing classifies an input and dispatches it to a specialized prompt or model. Parallelization runs calls side by side, either splitting a task into independent sections or voting across repeated attempts. Orchestrator-workers lets a central call split a task whose parts cannot be predicted in advance, and evaluator-optimizer loops a draft through a critic. At the top are agents, where the model itself decides each next step and tool call until the task is done.

Climb the ladder only as far as the evidence requires. Workflows give predictability, easy auditing and stable cost, so they suit well-defined tasks such as a regulated intake process that always follows the same six steps. Agents suit open-ended problems whose number of steps cannot be known in advance, but they spend more tokens, take longer and compound errors, because a wrong early assumption feeds every later step. A prototype that already meets most of its target with one call and good retrieval should be improved by analyzing its failures, not by adding agents.

Good designs also decide where people sit. Put an approval gate in front of actions that are costly or hard to reverse, such as large refunds or deletions, and let reads and drafts flow freely. Add loop guards (a turn limit and a spend limit), checkpoints that verify intermediate results, and durable state so a long run can resume instead of restarting. Close the loop by capturing reviewers' corrections: they become your evaluation set and the raw material for the next prompt or retrieval change.

Finally, tie every decision to a business value pillar: efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, or performance against service levels. Routing simple tickets to a small model and caching shared context serve cost, streaming and a latency budget serve performance, and automating a manual step serves efficiency. Report in the sponsor's terms, such as cost per resolved ticket and 95th-percentile response time, and compare designs on cost per completed task rather than price per token.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to solution design? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a restaurant kitchen. One skilled cook who can check the pantry and use the equipment is an augmented LLM. A fixed assembly line of prep, cook, plate and inspect is a workflow: the order never changes and each station can be checked. A head chef who reads each unusual order and decides which cooks to call in is orchestrator-workers. A chef who improvises an entire banquet on the fly is an agent: flexible, but you want a manager to approve any expensive purchase before the money is spent.
commonTraps: Choosing an agent because the problem sounds complex: if the steps are known and must be auditable, a workflow is the better answer.
Treating orchestrator-workers and sectioning as the same thing: sectioning splits work in advance in code, while orchestrator-workers lets the model decide the subtasks at run time.
Gating every step with a human, or none at all: approval gates belong on irreversible or high-impact actions, chosen by blast radius.
Justifying a design by token price alone: the exam expects cost per completed task, latency against a target and other business measures.
lessons.scenario: A freight forwarder wants staff to answer shipping-exception emails faster. The architect maps the business sentence to inputs (the email and the shipment record), processing (one augmented call with a lookup tool and policy text in a cached prefix), output (a draft reply) and feedback (staff edits stored for evaluation). Because a person approves each reply, no agent loop is needed. Success is reported as handle time per email and cost per resolved exception, and the team agrees to revisit routing or an agent design only if measured failures demand it.
lessons.onTheJob: In discovery meetings, sponsors rarely say 'workflow' or 'agent'. They say 'it should just handle it'. Translate that into explicit decisions: which steps are fixed, which need judgment, which actions are irreversible and who owns the exceptions. Sketch the input, processing, output and feedback path on one page before naming any pattern, and add a line per step on how its output will be checked. Teams that skip this tend to start with the most autonomous design and discover its cost in the first invoice. Start with the simplest design, instrument it, and let evidence promote it.

lessons.title: Multi-Agent Systems, Decomposition and Hosting Choices
lessons.summary: When several agents beat one, how to decompose work by context, how delegation really works, the orchestrator and advisor cost patterns, and who should run the loop.
lessons.reading:
A single well-designed agent with the right tools does more than most teams expect, and every extra agent adds a prompt to maintain, a hand-off to lose context in and a bill to pay. In Anthropic's testing, multi-agent designs used roughly three to ten times the tokens of a single agent, and its research system used about fifteen times a chat. Three situations justify the cost. First, context pollution: one subtask produces bulky output that is irrelevant to the next and degrades reasoning. Second, parallelizable work, such as researching thirty independent sources. Third, specialization, where focused tools and instructions beat one agent juggling dozens of tools. Before splitting for the third reason, try tool search, which can fix tool overload without a second agent.

How you split matters more than whether you split. Anthropic recommends a context-centric view: draw boundaries where context can truly be separated, such as independent research paths, components behind clean interfaces, or a verifier that only runs tests. The common mistake is problem-centric decomposition, a planner, implementer, tester and reviewer passing work along. Each hand-off loses the reasoning behind earlier steps, a telephone game that can cost more tokens in coordination than in work. The agent that builds a feature should usually write its tests too. A verification subagent is the split that works, because checking an artifact against explicit criteria needs little of the builder's history.

Delegation has mechanics worth knowing. A subagent starts with a fresh context, and the only thing it receives from its parent is the task prompt, so that prompt must carry the objective, file paths, constraints, output format and task boundaries; vague briefs make helpers duplicate each other's searches. The subagent explores in its own window and returns a condensed result, often one or two thousand tokens, which keeps the lead's context clean.

Cost patterns come in two shapes. In the orchestrator strategy a stronger model plans while lower-cost workers do bulk work; it saved money in Anthropic's measurements for routine work with a long cost tail and for work larger than one context window, not for a single dependent chain. In the advisor strategy a cheaper executor consults a stronger model at hard moments, but it helps only if the executor actually consults, so measure the consult rate against the executor alone at higher effort.

Finally, choose who runs the loop. With the Messages API you write the loop, tools and state. The Agent SDK gives you Claude Code's loop, tools, permissions and hooks as a library inside a process you operate. Claude Managed Agents, in beta, hosts the harness: you define an agent, an environment (a cloud sandbox or a self-hosted one) and sessions, then stream events. It offers subagents with persistent threads (one level deep, with a cap on child threads), dynamic workflows that run many agents in the background, and an advisor. Add a session budget as a hard cost ceiling, and remember that Managed Agents is stateful and currently not eligible for zero data retention or HIPAA coverage, which can decide the platform on its own.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to multi-agent design? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a consulting firm. A senior partner who takes a small engagement alone is a single agent. For a huge market study she hires associates, each handed a written brief and a clean desk, who come back with a two-page summary instead of their whole archive. If she split a small job into a planner, a writer and a checker, they would spend more time passing notes than working. The firm can rent a fully staffed office (Managed Agents), put the partner's playbook in your own office (the Agent SDK), or run everything by hand (the Messages API).
commonTraps: A subagent does not inherit the lead's conversation, so a vague one-line delegation produces duplicated or lost work.
Splitting by job title (planner, tester, reviewer) feels natural but is problem-centric and loses context at every hand-off; split along context boundaries instead.
Parallel subagents buy coverage, not necessarily speed, and multi-agent runs use several times the tokens, so they need tasks valuable enough to pay for it.
Workflow-run threads in Managed Agents cannot receive follow-up messages, whereas subagent threads can.
Cost caps belong in the platform (session budgets, turn and spend limits), not in a prompt asking the agent to be frugal.
lessons.scenario: A consultancy builds a competitive-intelligence assistant that compares twelve vendors. Each vendor is researched in parallel by a subagent that receives a written brief (objective, sources, output format, boundaries) and returns a 1,500-token summary with citations. The lead synthesizes the twelve summaries, and a verification subagent checks every claim against its cited source. A session budget caps each run, and a reviewer approves the report before it leaves the firm. The team rejected a planner-writer-reviewer chain because earlier prototypes lost context at each hand-off.
lessons.onTheJob: Treat multi-agent designs as an optimization you earn. Start with one agent and a good tool set, log where it fails, and split only along a boundary you can name: independent research paths, separate components or a black-box verifier. Write each delegation brief like a ticket for a contractor who has never seen the project, and have helpers return structured findings with sources. Set a session budget, a turn limit and a stop condition before the first long run, because one runaway loop can cost more than the whole prototyping phase. When stakeholders ask for 'a team of agents', ask which of the three situations (pollution, parallelism, specialization) it solves.

lessons.title: Models, Prompts, Context and Caching
lessons.summary: Choosing a model tier and effort with evidence, writing system prompts and examples, enforcing rules in code, managing the context window and reusing prompts through caching and Skills.
lessons.reading:
Model choice is a measured trade-off, not a loyalty. The current lineup runs from Claude Haiku 5.5 (fastest and lowest priced, for classification, extraction, routing and sub-agent work) through Sonnet 5.5 (best balance of speed and intelligence) and Opus 5.5 (long-running agentic and knowledge work, the usual starting point) to Fable 5.1 (the most capable open to all customers). Start small and move up when evaluations show a gap, or start strong and optimize down. Before switching models, sweep the effort parameter (low, medium, high, xhigh, max), which governs thinking, tool calls and self-checking inside one model. Compare options on cost per completed task, not price per token, and treat model IDs as pinned snapshots: an upgrade begins with a prompt audit, because newer models obey leftover instructions such as 'verify twice' literally.

A system prompt sets role, rules, tone and format. Aim for the right altitude: clear goals and a few heuristics, not a thicket of if-then rules that contradict each other. Explain why a rule matters. Zero-shot prompting, instructions alone, is the default; when judgment or format is inconsistent, add three to five relevant, diverse examples wrapped in tags. Use XML-style tags to separate instructions, documents and examples, and for long inputs put the documents first and the question last. For reasoning, current models think adaptively, steered by effort; prompts that ask for written-out reasoning can be declined, so ask for the answer plus a short justification.

Wording is guidance, not control. If a limit must hold, such as a refund ceiling, enforce it in the tool or back end, remove tools the role does not need, and use structured outputs (a JSON Schema in output_config.format, or strict tool use) when a downstream system rejects malformed data. Prefilled assistant turns are not supported on recent models.

The context window holds everything the model reads and writes: system prompt, tool definitions, messages, tool results and output, including thinking. A million tokens is available, but recall degrades as it fills (context rot), so curate. Count tokens before sending large inputs. The max_tokens cap is invisible to the model, so ask for short answers in the prompt; output tokens cost several times input tokens. For long runs, clear stale tool results with context editing, summarize with server-side compaction, or keep notes in files with the memory tool.

Reuse starts with prompt caching. The cache matches an exact prefix in the order tools, system, messages, so put stable content first and per-request text last. Up to four breakpoints mark where caching ends; a five-minute write costs 1.25 times base input, a one-hour write 2 times, and reads cost a fraction. Editing a tool, the system prompt or effort settings invalidates what follows, so add mid-conversation instructions with a system-role message. Build prompts from modules, and package specialist procedures as Agent Skills, whose names and descriptions are always loaded while their instructions load on demand.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to prompting and context? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Imagine briefing a new contractor. You hand over a one-page brief (the system prompt) with the goal and a few rules of thumb, plus a couple of sample jobs (examples). Long reference binders (documents) go at the top of the desk and today's question comes last. You do not shout 'NEVER' about money limits; you set the limit in the payment system. Photocopying the same binder every morning (caching) saves time as long as nobody rearranges its pages. A bigger desk (the context window) helps, but a cluttered desk still slows the work.
commonTraps: Lowering max_tokens does not make answers shorter: the model cannot see it, so the answer is simply cut off.
A volatile value such as a timestamp at the start of the prompt turns every request into a cache write and no reads.
Asking the model to write out its reasoning is no longer the way to get chain-of-thought on current models; rely on adaptive thinking and effort.
Prompt wording is not a guarantee: when consequences are severe, enforce the rule in code or configuration.
Changing top-level effort or editing the system prompt mid-conversation invalidates cached content.
lessons.scenario: A retailer's support assistant sends a 12,000-token policy manual and tool definitions on every request. The team places the manual and tools first with a breakpoint, moves the date and the customer's question after it, and uses the one-hour lifetime because agents pause for minutes between questions. They route the 80 percent of simple tickets to the smallest tier at low effort, escalate hard cases, and enforce the refund ceiling in the refund tool instead of the prompt. A prompt audit before each model upgrade removed three leftover 'be maximally thorough' lines and cut cost per ticket without hurting accuracy.
lessons.onTheJob: Keep a small evaluation set that reflects real traffic and re-run it on every model, effort or prompt change: opinions about models age quickly, but your measurements do not. Version prompts like code, and keep them modular so the stable parts can be cached and the variable parts stay at the end. Watch the cache-read share in your usage data, because a sudden fall usually means someone edited the prefix. Do not carry settings from one model to the next without a fresh effort sweep, since levels are recalibrated between generations. And whenever a requirement says 'must never', ask where in code it will be enforced.

lessons.title: Tools, MCP and Securing the Connection
lessons.summary: Trimming tool and agent configuration, choosing between direct calls, MCP and agent-to-agent integration, closing authentication and authorization gaps, and picking a cloud platform.
lessons.reading:
Integration problems usually start with too much capability. Capability bloat means an agent holds tools, permissions or instructions its job never needs; the symptoms are wrong-tool calls, large baseline token counts and a role that could do damage it should never be able to do. The fix is least privilege applied to configuration: remove what the role does not need rather than keeping it and adding logging or confirmation prompts, and prefer an allowlist (disable everything by default, enable named tools) over a denylist, which switches on every tool a server adds later. For the tools that remain, write rich descriptions saying what each does, when to use it and when not to, and what it does not return, and consolidate related operations. For large catalogs, defer definitions and let tool search load them on demand.

Next, pick the mechanism. A direct API or CLI call is simplest when one service calls one known system in a deterministic step. The Model Context Protocol earns its place when many clients must share an integration with consistent authentication: a host runs one client per server, and servers expose tools (model-controlled), resources (application-controlled) and prompts (user-controlled). Local servers use the stdio transport and shared remote servers use Streamable HTTP. The Messages API MCP connector, a beta feature, reaches a public HTTPS server directly but supports tool calls only. Agent-to-agent integration fits a counterpart that is itself an autonomous agent with its own tools and context. The 2026-07-28 MCP revision made the protocol stateless: no initialize handshake or protocol-level sessions, with capabilities carried on each request.

Authentication proves who is calling; authorization decides what they may do. Never ship an API key in browser code. Prefer service accounts to personal keys for shared workloads, and where the platform has its own identity use Workload Identity Federation, which swaps a short-lived OIDC token for a short-lived Claude token. In Managed Agents, keep each user's third-party credentials in vaults. MCP authorization builds on OAuth 2.1: the server publishes protected resource metadata, clients use PKCE and the resource parameter, and tokens are audience-bound. A server must reject tokens meant for others and must never pass a client's token through to an upstream API. Enforce authorization where the data lives, for example with a tenant filter in the retrieval service, never by asking the model to behave.

Claude is also offered through cloud platforms. Claude in Amazon Bedrock is AWS-operated, follows AWS's release schedule and is the choice when AWS must be the sole data processor. Claude Platform on AWS is Anthropic-operated, with AWS identity and billing and fast access to new features. Google Cloud and Microsoft Foundry have their own endpoints and authentication, and each omits some Anthropic-only features, so verify support before committing. On Foundry the deployment name is the model value, and regional endpoints on Bedrock and Google Cloud cost about ten percent more than global ones.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to integration and security? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Picture a building's security desk. Handing a visitor every key and posting a sign that says 'please do not open the vault' is a bloated, prompt-only design; giving out only the keys a visitor needs is least privilege. A shared front-desk process that any department can use to issue visitor badges is like MCP; a one-off handshake between two colleagues is a direct API call; asking another department's manager to handle a case on their own authority is agent-to-agent. A badge that expires at the end of the day (a federated token) beats a master key under the doormat.
commonTraps: Keeping risky tools and adding logging or confirmation prompts is only a compensating control; if the role never needs the tool, remove it.
A denylist leaves newly added tools switched on, so the allowlist is the safer default.
The MCP connector supports only tool calls and needs a public HTTPS server, so it cannot reach a local stdio server.
Token passthrough is forbidden even over HTTPS: servers must accept only tokens issued for them and use separate upstream credentials.
Prompt caching does not shrink tool definitions in the window; scoping and deferral do.
lessons.scenario: A bank's operations assistant must read ticket data, search policies and, rarely, release payments. The architect gives each of three agent roles only its own tools, with an allowlist on the shared MCP server, defers rarely used definitions behind tool search and requires human approval for payment release. The MCP server uses OAuth with audience-bound tokens and calls the ledger API with its own credential. Because AWS must be the sole data processor, the team uses Claude in Amazon Bedrock, accepts that the MCP connector and Managed Agents are not offered there, and runs its own MCP client instead.
lessons.onTheJob: Inventory capabilities before launch: list every tool, scope and credential each agent holds, and delete anything without a named business reason. Review third-party MCP servers like any other dependency, since their tool descriptions and annotations are untrusted input you do not control. Put secrets in a manager or vault, use federation wherever the platform offers an identity, and keep authorization checks in the services that hold the data. When a requirement says 'integrate with X', ask how many clients need X, who authenticates, and whether X is a function or an agent, and the right mechanism usually follows.

lessons.title: RAG, Retrieval Strategy, Context Discovery and Observability
lessons.summary: Designing a RAG pipeline with sound chunking and indexing, matching retrieval to the data, choosing progressive discovery over monolithic context, tuning accuracy and latency, and monitoring at scale.
lessons.reading:
Retrieval-augmented generation grounds answers in your data by finding relevant passages at question time and adding them to the prompt. Ask first whether you need it. If the knowledge base fits comfortably in the window, a cached prompt is simpler and removes retrieval as a failure point; RAG earns its keep when the corpus is large or changes often. When you build it, the pipeline is: split documents into chunks, embed them with an embedding model (Anthropic offers none; its documentation points to providers such as Voyage AI), store the vectors, retrieve at query time, optionally rerank, and pass the best chunks with their sources to Claude. Chunking is a design decision: follow structure such as sections and clauses, keep modest overlap and carry headings or metadata with each chunk, because pieces that are too small lose meaning and pieces that are too large dilute relevance.

Match retrieval to the data and the question. Embeddings capture meaning but can blur exact strings such as part numbers, while BM25 matches exact terms, and a hybrid that merges both lists with rank fusion beats either alone. Contextual Retrieval prepends a short chunk-specific note, such as which company and quarter a sentence describes, before embedding and before building the BM25 index; in Anthropic's tests it cut failed retrievals by 49 percent, and by 67 percent with reranking over a wider candidate set. Tabular questions are computations, so upload the file and let the model query it with code execution instead of pasting rows. For fast-changing code, search the live repository just in time with glob and grep. Use search result or document blocks with citations when answers must be traceable.

The same thinking applies to instructions and tools. A monolithic context loads everything up front; it is fine for a 90,000-token manual used constantly, especially when cached, but it spends tokens every turn and invites context rot. Progressive discovery loads in stages: skills load names first and instructions on demand, tool search loads definitions when needed, and just-in-time retrieval keeps references and fetches content with tools. Choose by size, frequency of use, volatility and how sparsely each task touches the material.

Accuracy, latency and cost pull against each other, so justify settings with measurements. Smaller tiers and lower effort cut latency, streaming improves time to first token, caching shortens prefix processing, parallel and programmatic tool calls remove round trips, batch processing halves the price of work nobody waits on, and reranking adds a little latency for precision. When results are checkable, run low effort first and re-run only the failures at higher effort.

At scale you cannot read every conversation. Emit OpenTelemetry traces with spans for model requests and tool calls, track tokens, cache-read share, stop-reason mix and per-tool failures, keep request IDs, and alert on shifts. When answers degrade after a content change, inspect what was retrieved before blaming the model.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to RAG and retrieval? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a research librarian. A tiny reference shelf can sit on your desk, which is putting everything in the prompt. For a big library, the librarian uses an index by meaning (embeddings) and a card catalog by exact title (BM25), merges both lists, and has a senior librarian choose the best twenty (reranking). Each photocopied page carries a note saying which book and chapter it came from (contextual retrieval). For a spreadsheet you hand over the file and a calculator instead of reading numbers aloud. A dashboard at the front desk (observability) shows queues, wait times and which shelves keep failing.
commonTraps: Assuming RAG is always required: a corpus that fits in a cached prompt may not need it.
Believing Anthropic supplies embeddings: it does not, and Claude only consumes the retrieved text.
Fixing missed identifiers with bigger embeddings: exact strings need lexical (BM25) retrieval merged with the vector results.
Adding a reranker to repair recall: it can only reorder candidates that were already retrieved.
Pasting tabular data into the prompt for aggregate questions instead of using code execution over an uploaded file.
lessons.scenario: An insurer's claims assistant must answer questions over 40,000 policy documents, query claim records and look up part numbers. The team chunks policies by clause with the heading path as metadata, adds contextual notes, builds both a vector and a BM25 index, merges them with rank fusion, reranks 150 candidates to the best 20 and returns passages as search results with citations. Claim data is queried through a read-only tool, not embedded. Traces and metrics for tokens, cache reads, stop reasons and per-tool failures feed one dashboard, and a drop in answer accuracy after a content refresh sends engineers first to the retrieval logs.
lessons.onTheJob: Build the retrieval evaluation first: a set of real questions with the passages that should be found, scored on whether they appear in the top results. That separates retrieval failures from generation failures and tells you which lever to pull. Keep an eye on index freshness and on what a content refresh changed, log the retrieved chunk IDs with every answer, and resist adding components, since each stage costs latency. Before building a vector store, ask whether a cached prompt, a file with code execution, or a live search tool already fits the data shape.

lessons.title: Evaluation and Testing: Success Criteria, Test Sets, Graders and Regression
lessons.summary: Turning "good" into measurable criteria across accuracy, latency, cost and safety; building representative datasets with a held-out set; choosing code, human and model graders; error analysis, regression suites, and releasing with shadow mode, canaries and A/B tests. Covers exam Domain 4: define evaluation metrics, design datasets and test frameworks with mixed methodologies, conduct A/B testing and iterative improvement, and diagnose system issues.
lessons.reading:
Start with what 'good' means. A request such as 'accurate, fast and safe' cannot be tested, so the first task is to turn it into success criteria that are specific, measurable, achievable and relevant, across several dimensions at once. For claims triage that might be: at least 92 percent correct routing on 1,000 held-out claims, 95th-percentile response time under four seconds, cost under two cents per claim, and fewer than one output in a thousand flagged unsafe. Even hazy goals such as safety can be quantified. The dimensions trade off: a prompt that lifts accuracy but doubles latency and cost is not an improvement unless the other targets still hold.

Next comes the evaluation dataset: cases, each with an input and a reference answer or a grading rule. It should mirror the real task distribution, so sample anonymized production traffic and add deliberate hard cases such as missing fields, ambiguous requests, other languages and adversarial text. Anthropic favors volume with automated grading over a few perfect hand-graded cases. Keep a held-out test set that is never used while writing prompts, choosing examples or tuning rules. If failed evaluation cases are pasted into the prompt as few-shot examples, the test has leaked into the prompt: the score reads 98 percent while production delivers 86.

Grade with the cheapest method that is reliable. Code-based grading (exact match, schema validation, unit tests) is fast, deterministic and scales to every change, so use it wherever the answer is checkable. Human graders are the most flexible but slow and expensive; keep them for calibration and hard cases. For judgments that rules cannot make, such as tone, use a model grader with a written rubric of explicit, independently checkable criteria, a constrained verdict (a label or a 1-5 scale) and room to reason before it scores. Then calibrate it against human labels on a sample, and fix the rubric if agreement is low. Expect judge bias, such as favoring longer answers or the one listed first, and counter it by randomizing order.

Evaluation is a loop. Run a baseline, read a sample of failures and sort them by root cause: a retrieval miss, an ambiguous instruction, a skipped step, a wrong tool or truncation. Error analysis shows which fix removes the most failures; a step that must always happen belongs in code, not in a sentence the model may skip. Change one thing at a time and rerun. Keep a regression suite, a fixed versioned set that grows with every production incident and runs on each prompt, model, tool or retrieval change. Outputs vary from run to run, so repeat runs and compare intervals rather than single scores.

Offline results only show that a change is safe to try, so release in stages. Shadow mode runs the candidate on live inputs without showing or acting on its output. A canary exposes a small, watched slice of traffic and widens only while quality, latency, cost and safety hold. An A/B test randomly and consistently assigns concurrent users to the current and candidate versions, with the primary metric, guardrail metrics and sample size fixed beforehand. Comparing this week with last week, or stopping when one arm leads, are classic flawed designs, and a variant that breaks a guardrail does not ship as is.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to evaluation? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a driving test. The examiner does not ask 'are you a good driver?'. There is a written checklist (specific, measurable criteria), a route that includes tricky junctions instead of an empty car park (a representative dataset), and the route is not revealed in advance (a held-out set). Some items are scored by rule, such as whether you stopped at the line, while others need an examiner's judgment, so examiners are periodically compared with one another (calibration). Passing once does not end the story: spot checks keep standards up, and a new driver rides with an instructor before driving alone, much like shadow mode before a canary rollout.
commonTraps: Treating one headline metric as success: a gain in accuracy that breaks the latency, cost or safety targets is not shippable.
Tuning against the cases you report: a score on tuning cases, or on cases pasted into the prompt, measures memorization rather than production quality.
Reaching for a model grader by default: when the answer is checkable, code-based grading is faster and more reliable, and a model grader must be calibrated against human labels before it is trusted.
Calling a week-over-week comparison an A/B test, or stopping a test the moment one arm leads.
Fixing the symptom: switching to a bigger model or rewriting the whole prompt before reading the failures and finding the largest root-cause category.
lessons.scenario: A lender's assistant drafts replies to loan-application questions. The architect and the sponsor agree targets for correct policy answers, 95th-percentile response time, cost per reply and a cap on unsupported claims. The team samples anonymized past questions, adds hard cases (outdated policy, two languages, very long threads) and holds out a third of the set. Code checks the quoted policy identifiers; a rubric-driven model grader scores tone and groundedness after being calibrated on a human-labeled sample. Error analysis of the baseline shows most failures come from stale retrieval rather than wording, so the first change fixes the index. A regression suite gates every release, and each new version runs in shadow mode before a five percent canary.
lessons.onTheJob: Write the criteria down with the sponsor before building, and keep the numbers in the same document as the design; it settles arguments later. Treat every production incident as a free test case and add it to the regression suite the same day. Budget human time for calibration and for reading failures, because teams that skip error analysis tend to rewrite prompts at random. Keep graders and datasets under version control like code, so a score can always be tied to the exact versions that produced it. And report results with their spread: stakeholders trust 'between 88 and 91 percent over five runs' more than one impressive number that nobody can reproduce.

lessons.title: Optimization and Monitoring: Cost, Latency, Caching, Batching and Observability
lessons.summary: Measuring cost per completed task, pulling the main levers (prompt caching, batch processing, model tier and effort, output length, streaming), living within rate limits and spend caps, and monitoring quality, cost and drift with structured logs, traces and the Usage and Cost API. Covers exam Domain 4: optimize token usage, latency and cost-performance trade-offs, and monitor system performance using logging and observability tools.
lessons.reading:
Optimization starts with measurement, not tricks. Compare configurations on cost per completed task rather than price per token: a stronger model that finishes in fewer turns, or a cheaper model that fails often and needs retries, can reverse a price-list ranking, and failed attempts still bill their tokens. List the candidates (model tier, effort level, prompt, retrieval depth, caching), run each on your own evaluation set and plot pass rate against cost per task. The configurations that nothing beats on both axes form the cost-quality frontier; choose the cheapest one that clears your quality bar, and price the hardest tenth of tasks too, because the tail carries a large share of spend.

The biggest free lever is prompt caching. An agent resends its whole growing conversation on every turn, so cost climbs roughly with the square of the turn count, and caching the stable prefix makes each resend far cheaper. A cache write costs a premium over normal input (1.25 times for the five-minute lifetime, 2 times for the one-hour lifetime) and a read costs a small fraction of it (a tenth on most models, less on some). So a five-minute cache repays itself after one reuse and a one-hour cache after two. Keep the prefix identical, put per-request text last, and watch the share of input read from cache: a healthy loop reads well over 80 percent, and a sudden drop means the prefix changed. Cache reads also stay out of the input-token rate limit on most models.

The second lever is the Message Batches API: half price on every token for work that can finish within 24 hours (most batches take under an hour), with results matched to requests by custom id, not by order. Use it for evaluation runs, backfills and nightly jobs, never for a person who is waiting; streaming and fast mode are unavailable in a batch, and cache hits there are best effort, so prefer the one-hour cache duration. On interactive paths, trim the prompt and ask for sentence or paragraph limits (a hard max_tokens only truncates), pick the smallest model and effort level that pass your evaluation, and stream so text appears at once. Get a prompt working first, then cut latency one change at a time.

Plan for limits. Requests, input tokens and output tokens per minute are separate ceilings that refill continuously. A 429 with a retry-after header means wait that long; then use exponential backoff with jitter, ramp traffic gradually and move non-urgent work to batches. A monthly spend cap also returns a 429, but without retry-after, so retrying cannot help; lower workspace spend limits and alerts keep it from arriving unannounced.

Monitor what you optimize. Log a structured record for every call: model, prompt version, token usage including cached tokens, stop reason, latency, request id and tool outcomes. Store full prompts and responses only when needed and permitted; exported traces carry identifiers, timing and token counts by default, and full content is an opt-in that moves sensitive text into your observability vendor. Reconcile spend with the Usage and Cost Admin API, grouped by workspace, model or key. Then expect quality drift: schedule the regression suite, grade a sample of live traffic and alert on refusals, stop reasons and validator failures.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to optimization? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Picture running a delivery fleet. You judge the service by the cost of each completed delivery, not by the price of fuel per liter.
