Nurses paste case notes, which contain protected health information, into an internal tool, and the tool calls the Claude API to produce a summary that the nurse reviews before saving it. The organization enabled HIPAA readiness with a signed business associate agreement.

Last week the data team added two features in the same organization: a nightly job that sends the day's notes through batch processing to build a trend report, and a chart step that uses the code execution tool. Both now fail with 400 errors, and the team asks an administrator to 'turn HIPAA readiness off'.

Separately, an Anthropic notice says the model the tool pins will be retired in about two months, with a named replacement. Nobody owns the migration, the prompt lives in a shared document that several people edit, and there is no evaluation set; the only quality evidence is nurse complaints. Finally, executives want the summaries to start recommending whether each claim should be approved, with nurses handling only exceptions.

questions.question: What is the right response to the 400 errors?
options: Ask the administrator to disable HIPAA readiness until the new features are live, and enable it again once the trend report is built
Enable zero data retention on the organization as well, which makes batch processing and code execution eligible under the business associate agreement
Keep HIPAA readiness, since the API is blocking features outside coverage, and run the trend and chart work in a separate organization on de-identified data
Retry the failing calls with a different API key from the same workspace, since the 400 errors are caused by the key rather than by the features
questions.explanation: The 400 errors show HIPAA readiness doing its job: the API rejects features outside coverage (batch processing and code execution are not eligible), so protected health information cannot reach them by accident. An administrator cannot disable HIPAA readiness once it is enabled, and zero data retention is a separate arrangement that does not make those features eligible either. A different key does not change the organization's rules. The compliant paths are a separate organization for work that needs those features, using de-identified data, or redesigning the work with eligible features.

questions.question: Which two actions belong in the first weeks of the migration plan? (Choose two.)
options: Name an owner, and inventory every use of the pinned model by API key and model from the Console usage export
Build an evaluation set from nurse-reviewed cases, version the prompt, and run the old and new models side by side
Change the model ID in production now, and let nurse complaints show what breaks
Wait until the last week so that the replacement's documentation is as mature as possible
Pause the tool for all nurses until the migration is finished
questions.explanation: Nobody owns the migration, nothing is inventoried, the prompt is unversioned and there is no evaluation set, so the first weeks should create those foundations: an owner and a usage inventory, then an evaluation set and a versioned prompt so that the old and new models can be compared before any live exposure. Using nurses as the test bed puts patient-facing work at risk, waiting leaves no time to fix regressions, and pausing the tool removes value without reducing the retirement risk.

questions.question: How should the request for approval recommendations be handled?
options: Let the model decide claims below a dollar threshold automatically, and publish a general privacy notice on the insurer's website with a link to the complaints process
Proceed only with a qualified reviewer who meaningfully checks each recommendation and can change it, claimants told AI was used, and subgroup results tracked
Add a step in which the model double-checks its own approval recommendation, and let nurses skip review when the two answers match
Decline the request, because Anthropic's usage policy forbids any use of Claude in insurance or healthcare decisions, and ask the executives to wait for a policy change
questions.explanation: Insurance and access to healthcare are high-risk areas in Anthropic's usage policy. Use is permitted with two safeguards: a qualified person must meaningfully review each recommendation with authority to change it, and affected individuals must be told that AI was used. Subgroup evaluation guards against unequal outcomes. A threshold-based automatic decision, a self-check and a privacy notice each remove or replace the human review, and the policy does not ban the use outright.

compare.scenario: A contract-review pipeline must flag risky clauses. Missing a risky clause is far more costly than a false alarm, and there is no single gold-standard rubric to iterate against. Which pattern fits better?
compare.optionA: Parallel voting: several differently prompted reviewers analyze the contract independently, and a clause is flagged if enough of them flag it
compare.optionB: Evaluator-optimizer: one reviewer drafts a list of risky clauses and a critic keeps refining it until the critic is satisfied
compare.why: Voting gives diverse, independent attempts and a tunable threshold that trades false negatives against false alarms, which matches costly misses with no crisp rubric. Evaluator-optimizer is the tempting runner-up because it sounds more rigorous, but it needs clear criteria and measurable improvement from feedback, and a single reviewer plus a critic can share the same blind spot.

compare.scenario: A single agent has 45 tools across CRM, marketing and messaging systems. Any one request uses at most five of them, domains rarely mix, and the team's only complaints are high token usage and occasional wrong-tool choices. What should they try first?
compare.optionA: Defer the tool definitions and add tool search, so only the needed ones load for each request
compare.optionB: Split into three specialist subagents behind an orchestrator that routes each request
compare.why: The problem is tool overload, which tool search addresses directly without new agents, prompts or routing errors to maintain. Specialist subagents are the tempting runner-up and do help when domains need different instructions or personas, but they add coordination cost, misrouting risk and several times the tokens, so they come second.

compare.scenario: A pricing analysis has seven steps, each needing the result of the one before, and the whole job fits comfortably inside one context window. The team wants to reduce cost. Which approach is better?
compare.optionA: Run one capable model through the whole chain and sweep a lower effort level
compare.optionB: Use an orchestrator that hands each step to a lower-cost worker model
compare.why: For a single dependent chain that fits in one window, Anthropic's measurements found the strong model alone at lower effort came out ahead. The orchestrator is the tempting runner-up because workers are cheaper per token, but each hand-off repeats context and adds coordination, and delegation paid off only for routine work with a long cost tail or work larger than one window.

compare.scenario: An agent on the Opus tier meets its quality targets but costs too much, and nobody has yet tested alternatives. Which first move is better?
compare.optionA: Run an effort sweep on the same model against the evaluation set and keep the cheapest level that holds quality
compare.optionB: Move the whole workload to the smallest tier and see what happens
compare.why: Effort changes thinking, tool calls and self-checking inside one model and is often a better lever than switching models, and the evaluation set shows exactly where quality drops. Moving to the smallest tier is the tempting runner-up and may be right for easy, checkable work, but doing it blind changes capability and prompt behavior at once and makes failures hard to attribute.

compare.scenario: A procurement assistant must never approve a purchase over $10,000 without a manager. The system prompt says so in capital letters, and a test showed it holding in 500 of 500 attempts. Auditors want assurance against adversarial input. Which control is better?
compare.optionA: Check the amount in the approval tool and refuse to run above the threshold without a manager approval token
compare.optionB: Keep the prompt rule and add ten more examples of refusing large purchases
compare.why: A check in code holds no matter what the model is persuaded to say, which is the assurance an auditor needs. Prompt rules and examples are the tempting runner-up because they passed 500 of 500 tests, but a passing sample is not a guarantee, and where consequences are severe programmatic enforcement beats prompt-based guidance.

compare.scenario: A read-only reporting assistant connects to a vendor's MCP server with forty tools, and the vendor ships new tools every few weeks. Which toolset configuration is better?
compare.optionA: Allowlist: disable all tools by default and enable only the named read tools
compare.optionB: Denylist: leave tools on by default and disable the known write and delete tools
compare.why: An allowlist keeps the role limited to what it needs, including after the vendor adds tools. A denylist is the tempting runner-up because it is quicker to write, but every new tool is switched on automatically, so the exposure grows without any review.

compare.scenario: A company wants 200 employees' assistants to use an internal ticketing integration, with central updates, central logging and per-user permissions. Which MCP deployment is better?
compare.optionA: A centrally hosted server over Streamable HTTP with OAuth authorization
compare.optionB: A stdio server that each employee installs and runs locally
compare.why: A shared remote server gives one place to update, log and authorize, with per-user tokens through OAuth. Local stdio is the tempting runner-up because it is simple for one developer and needs no network service, but it multiplies installations, versions and credentials across 200 machines and takes credentials from each environment instead of a central authorization flow.

compare.scenario: A team generates one-paragraph summaries of support cases. Many different wordings are acceptable, no single reference summary exists for most cases, and the team wants an automated quality score on every release. Which grading approach fits better?
compare.optionA: A model grader with a rubric of checkable criteria (covers the cause, the resolution and the customer's request, with no invented facts), calibrated on a human-labeled sample
compare.optionB: String-overlap scoring against a single reference summary written by an analyst for each case, computed by code on every release
compare.why: Valid summaries can differ in wording, so a rubric-based model grader that has been calibrated against human labels can judge the properties that matter, at scale. Overlap scoring is the tempting runner-up because it is cheap and deterministic, and code-based grading is the right choice when an answer is checkable, but here it penalizes correct paraphrases and rewards copied wording, so the score tracks phrasing rather than quality.

compare.scenario: A finance team summarizes 40,000 filings every night for a morning report due at 7 a.m. The current model tier meets the quality target in evaluation, and the team wants to cut cost without risking that target. Which approach is better?
compare.optionA: Send the filings through the Message Batches API with the same model, using identical cache_control blocks on the shared instructions
compare.optionB: Keep the synchronous calls but switch to a cheaper model tier that has not been evaluated on these filings
compare.why: Batching halves the price of every token with no change to quality, and a nightly job can wait for results (most batches finish within an hour, and the maximum is 24), so the validated model is kept. A cheaper tier is the tempting runner-up because its per-token price is lower, but it trades an unmeasured quality risk for savings that batching already delivers; if the team wants to try it, it must first pass the same evaluation.

compare.scenario: A 40-person startup on Claude Teams has no device management. It wants a shared permission baseline and an approved-MCP list applied to every developer's Claude Code starting today. Which delivery is better?
compare.optionA: Server-managed settings configured once in the claude.ai admin console, which Claude Code fetches at startup and refreshes hourly
compare.optionB: A managed-settings.json file copied by hand onto each developer's machine and kept in sync by the team itself
compare.why: Without MDM, the console route needs no device management and reaches everyone within about an hour of a change. A hand-copied file is the tempting runner-up because the operating system protects a system-directory file better, but without configuration tooling nobody keeps 40 laptops in sync, and developers who are local administrators can edit it anyway. If auditors later require tamper resistance, the company can move to MDM-delivered settings.

compare.scenario: A zero-data-retention organization must classify 50,000 sensitive documents overnight. Cost matters, but the documents must stay out of Anthropic's storage. Which approach is better?
compare.optionA: Send the documents through the Message Batches API to get the 50 percent discount
compare.optionB: Send them as synchronous requests at controlled concurrency, with prompt caching for the shared instructions
compare.why: Batch processing is not eligible for zero data retention because it stores requests and results, and nothing blocks the request, so the data would silently leave the arrangement. Batch is the tempting runner-up because of its price discount, which is the right trade for non-sensitive, latency-tolerant work; here the retention requirement dominates, and caching recovers part of the cost.

compare.scenario: An agent summarizes inbound supplier emails and can also issue payments. Red-team emails with planted instructions sometimes get it to start a payment. Which control is better?
compare.optionA: Remove the payment tool from the email-reading agent, and route payments through a separate step that requires human approval
compare.optionB: Add a strong untrusted-content policy to the system prompt, and keep the payment tool available to the agent
compare.why: Removing the capability and gating the action shrinks the blast radius, so even a successful injection cannot move money. The system prompt policy is the tempting runner-up and belongs in the design as one layer, but model behavior is not a security control, so it cannot be the only protection for an irreversible action.

compare.scenario: A chatbot started misbehaving on Tuesday after a prompt edit, and customers are noticing. Prompt versions are stored and a feature flag controls which version is live. What should the on-call engineer do first?
compare.optionA: Edit the live prompt to patch the misbehavior, and keep testing in production until the answers look right
compare.optionB: Switch the flag back to the previous prompt version, then investigate offline using request IDs and logs
compare.why: Restoring the last known-good version contains the incident in seconds and gives the team time to diagnose without customers watching, which is why versioning and flags exist. A live hot-fix is the tempting runner-up because it feels like progress, but unreviewed edits under pressure can add new failures and destroy the evidence of what went wrong.

compare.scenario: Before a pilot, a hospital's clinical lead asks how accurate the documentation assistant will be. Which answer sets expectations better?
compare.optionA: 'On 400 reviewed sample notes it was correct on 93 percent; here are the typical errors, which ones validation catches, and the review step that stays in place'
compare.optionB: 'The model scored very highly on public medical benchmarks, so you can expect excellent accuracy on your notes'
compare.why: A measured result on representative cases, with failure examples and the remaining human control, gives the lead something to check and trust. Public benchmark scores are the tempting runner-up because they are impressive and easy to cite, but they do not describe this workload and set an expectation the system may not meet.
